title: West Palm Beach residents protest 'ultra-rich' investment conference: 'This is our city' - NewsBreak
text:
By Andrew Marra ,
1 days ago WEST PALM BEACH ‚Äî Fifty protesters marched through CityPlace as a global investment conference kicked off in the downtown entertainment district, denouncing the event as a sign of the city‚Äôs continuing transformation into a ‚Äúplayground for the ultra-rich.‚Äù
The protesters were targeting the Feb. 2 start of WSJ Invest Live , a two-day event run by the Wall Street Journal and sponsored by Related Ross, West Palm Beach‚Äôs largest development firm and the owner of CityPlace.
The activists, who said they convened the protest through informal online groups such as the Anti-Trump Action Coalition and the Florida Socialist Alternative, said they were hoping to put a stop to what they called the overdevelopment of West Palm and the rest of Palm Beach County.
Protester Dominick Arrieux called the Wall Street Journal event ‚Äúthe showroom for a decade-long project to displace residents from their communities and to auction off West Palm to Silicon Valley tech CEOs, financial firms and defense contractors.‚Äù
‚ÄúThe billionaires behind these plans want to pitch their version of West Palm as a safe haven for the ruling class, transforming our city into a playground for the ultra-rich,‚Äù he said in comments to the gathered crowd
‚ÄúBut this is our city,‚Äù he continued. ‚ÄúWe‚Äôre here today to make that clear ‚Äî that the people of West Palm won‚Äôt be quiet while they take over our neighborhoods.‚Äù
The protest started at 7 p.m. Feb. 2 with participants demonstrating in the median at the corner of Okeechobee Boulevard and Rosemary Avenue, carrying signs sayings ‚ÄúNo Wall Street South !‚Äù and chanting ‚ÄúHey hey, ho ho, billionaires have got to go.‚Äù
After a half-hour, they marched up Rosemary into CityPlace and chanted outside the Eataly food hall, where the Wall Street Journal‚Äôs publisher was scheduled to give welcoming remarks to kick off the event, billed as the newspaper's ‚Äúpremier event for the global investment community.‚Äù
They chanted there for several minutes before marching back to Okeechobee Boulevard and disbanding.
Some participants said they felt compelled to speak out because of the steep rise in rents and the cost of living they‚Äôve experienced in recent years.
‚ÄúWest Palm Beach is changing so drastically, and it‚Äôs not for the people of West Palm Beach who are born and raised here,‚Äù said Janelle, a city resident who declined to give her last name. ‚ÄúAll the people sticking their hands in, making it their playground are pushing people out of their homes.‚Äù
Andrew Marra is a reporter at The Palm Beach Post. Reach him at amarra@pbpost.com .
